Reply naturally in English as the Patient to the last Doctor utterance.\nAnswer only the question, in 2–3 sentences maximum.\n\n[Dialogue]\nDoctor: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?\n\nPatient: It's a bit embarrassing to admit, but lately I just can't stop dwelling on how my face and body look as I'm aging. It has gotten to the point where it's making me avoid normal daily activities that I used to do without even thinking twice. I just feel so anxious about it all the time now.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what specifically about your face and body is causing you distress, and how often you find yourself thinking about these concerns?\n\nPatient: Whenever I look in the mirror, all I can see are these sagging lines around my mouth and my neck starting to droop, like my whole face is just collapsing. It's almost constant, and I find myself constantly dwelling on it and worrying that everyone at work is noticing how old and worn-out I look.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself engaging in repetitive behaviors, such as excessive mirror checking, grooming, or trying to hide your perceived flaws, in an attempt to alleviate your anxiety about your appearance?\n\nPatient: Yes, I do that a lot. I also change outfits repeatedly to hide my neck and arms, and I'm constantly asking my husband if I look too old before I can force myself out the door.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your concerns about your appearance are grounded in a realistic fear of being perceived as old or unattractive by others, or do you think there might be something medically wrong with your body that you're trying to hide or fix?\n\nPatient: It's definitely a fear of being perceived as old, worn-out, and unattractive by others, especially when I'm at work. I don't think it's a medical illness, and my primary care doctor actually did some physical exams and found nothing medically wrong with me. Still, I just can't stop worrying about how everyone else sees my aging face and neck.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant weight fluctuations or do you have a fear of gaining weight that contributes to your distress about your appearance?\n\nPatient: No, weight fluctuations or gaining weight aren't really the issue for me. My distress is completely focused on the signs of aging, like the sagging skin on my neck and face. I'm just worried about looking old and worn out, rather than my weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your fear of looking old is primarily driven by concerns about being perceived as unattractive or if you believe there's something fundamentally wrong with your body that needs to be fixed?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure which of those two it is, and I haven't thought about it in those exact terms. I just feel completely overwhelmed by how collapsed and worn-out my face looks, and I simply dread having other people see me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could somehow completely fix or hide the signs of aging on your face and neck, your anxiety and distress would significantly decrease or even disappear?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely, because my anxiety, avoiding work, and those long morning routines are entirely driven by how I look. I truly believe that if I could just fix or hide the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck, all of this distress would disappear and my life would go right back to normal.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a specific situation where you felt your appearance was acceptable or you didn't worry about it, and how that differed from your current experiences?\n\nPatient: I can't really think of a specific situation recently where I felt my appearance was acceptable. But in the past, before these aging concerns started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and simply didn't think or worry about my looks at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about your appearance or engaging in behaviors to try to improve it, and how has this impacted your daily life and relationships?\n\nPatient: Every morning I lose nearly an hour stuck in front of the mirror applying makeup, checking my phone camera, and constantly asking my husband for reassurance. This has caused me to show up late to work, turn down important presentations, and cancel social plans like my book club. My primary care doctor actually ran physical exams and found everything was completely normal. All of my distress is really just about looking so \"old and worn-out\" and the constant fear of others noticing these signs of aging on my face and neck.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have ever considered or sought cosmetic procedures, such as plastic surgery, to address your concerns about your appearance?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really sought out or seriously considered plastic surgery or cosmetic procedures. I've mostly just been trying to manage everything on my own by using makeup and changing my outfits to cover things up.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your primary concern is the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive by others, or if you genuinely believe that there's something fundamentally wrong with your body that needs to be fixed, even though your doctor has found nothing medically wrong?\n\nPatient: Since my primary care doctor found me physically healthy, I know it's not a medical disease. My distress is purely about how I look—I feel completely consumed by how old, sagging, and worn-out my face and neck appear. I'm constantly worried that others at work and in public are noticing these flaws and judging me, even when they tell me they don't see anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that others actually notice and care about the signs of aging on your face and neck as much as you do, or do you believe they are just being polite when they tell you that you look fine?"

It has gotten to the point where it's making me avoid normal daily activities that I used to do without even thinking twice. I just feel so anxious about it all the time now.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what specifically about your face and body is causing you distress, and how often you find yourself thinking about these concerns?\n\nPatient: Whenever I look in the mirror, all I can see are these sagging lines around my mouth and my neck starting to droop, like my whole face is just collapsing. It's almost constant, and I find myself constantly dwelling on it and worrying that everyone at work is noticing how old and worn-out I look.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself engaging in repetitive behaviors, such as excessive mirror checking, grooming, or trying to hide your perceived flaws, in an attempt to alleviate your anxiety about your appearance?\n\nPatient: Yes, I do that a lot. Most mornings I lose almost an hour putting on and wiping off makeup, tilting my head under the light, and zooming in on my face with my phone camera. I also change outfits repeatedly to hide my neck and arms, and I'm constantly asking my husband if I look too old before I can force myself out the door.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your concerns about your appearance are grounded in a realistic fear of being perceived as old or unattractive by others, or do you think there might be something medically wrong with your body that you're trying to hide or fix?\n\nPatient: It's definitely a fear of being perceived as old, worn-out, and unattractive by others, especially when I'm at work. I don't think it's a medical illness, and my primary care doctor actually did some physical exams and found nothing medically wrong with me. Still, I just can't stop worrying about how everyone else sees my aging face and neck.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant weight fluctuations or do you have a fear of gaining weight that contributes to your distress about your appearance?\n\nPatient: No, weight fluctuations or gaining weight aren't really the issue for me. My distress is completely focused on the signs of aging, like the sagging skin on my neck and face. I'm just worried about looking old and worn out, rather than my weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your fear of looking old is primarily driven by concerns about being perceived as unattractive or if you believe there's something fundamentally wrong with your body that needs to be fixed?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure which of those two it is, and I haven't thought about it in those exact terms. I just feel completely overwhelmed by how collapsed and worn-out my face looks, and I simply dread having other people see me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could somehow completely fix or hide the signs of aging on your face and neck, your anxiety and distress would significantly decrease or even disappear?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely, because my anxiety, avoiding work, and those long morning routines are entirely driven by how I look. I truly believe that if I could just fix or hide the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck, all of this distress would disappear and my life would go right back to normal.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a specific situation where you felt your appearance was acceptable or you didn't worry about it, and how that differed from your current experiences?\n\nPatient: I can't really think of a specific situation recently where I felt my appearance was acceptable. But in the past, before these aging concerns started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and simply didn't think or worry about my looks at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about your appearance or engaging in behaviors to try to improve it, and how has this impacted your daily life and relationships?\n\nPatient: Every morning I lose nearly an hour stuck in front of the mirror applying makeup, checking my phone camera, and constantly asking my husband for reassurance. This has caused me to show up late to work, turn down important presentations, and cancel social plans like my book club. It is really straining my personal life and has even made my supervisor hint that I'm becoming unreliable.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever worry that your perceived flaws in appearance might be a sign of an underlying medical condition, or is your concern solely about the cosmetic and social implications of how you look?\n\nPatient: My concern is entirely about the cosmetic aspect and how others perceive me, rather than any kind of medical illness. My primary care doctor actually ran physical exams and found everything was completely normal. All of my distress is really just about looking so \"old and worn-out\" and the constant fear of others noticing these signs of aging on my face and neck.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have ever considered or sought cosmetic procedures, such as plastic surgery, to address your concerns about your appearance?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really sought out or seriously considered plastic surgery or cosmetic procedures. I've mostly just been trying to manage everything on my own by using makeup and changing my outfits to cover things up.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your primary concern is the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive by others, or if you genuinely believe that there's something fundamentally wrong with your body that needs to be fixed, even though your doctor has found nothing medically wrong?\n\nPatient: Since my primary care doctor found me physically healthy, I know it's not a medical disease. My distress is purely about how I look—I feel completely consumed by how old, sagging, and worn-out my face and neck appear. I'm constantly worried that others at work and in public are noticing these flaws and judging me, even when they tell me they don't see anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that others actually notice and care about the signs of aging on your face and neck as much as you do, or do you believe they are just being polite when they tell you that you look fine?\n\nPatient: I honestly believe they are just being polite to spare my feelings. I have this deep-seated feeling that everyone at work must be noticing how old and worn-out I look, even if they claim otherwise just to make me feel better.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance are more about fearing you have a serious illness or condition that's making you look old, or is it purely about the cosmetic and social impact of how you look to others?\n\nPatient: It is purely about the cosmetic and social impact, not because I'm worried about having a medical illness. I am deeply self-conscious about looking old, worn-out, and sagging, and my main dread is that others will notice these flaws and judge me. That fear is exactly why I've been avoiding presentations at work, video calls, and social gatherings.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any periods in your life where your concerns about your appearance significantly decreased or disappeared for a while, only to return later?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really had ups and downs or periods where this went away and came back. It has just been a gradual, steady worsening over the last few years as I've gotten older and taken on a more public role at work. Before this started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and didn't worry about my appearance at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any other aspects of your appearance, besides the signs of aging on your face and neck, that you are excessively concerned about or spend a significant amount of time thinking about?\n\nPatient: Yes, I also worry about my arms looking older and flabby. That's a big reason why I spend so much time changing outfits every morning, trying to find clothes that cover both my neck and my arms before I go out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your excessive concerns about your appearance, particularly the signs of aging, interfere with your daily life, relationships, and overall well-being, and do you feel that these concerns are disproportionate to any actual flaws in your appearance?"

This has caused me to show up late to work, turn down important presentations, and cancel social plans like my book club. It is really straining my personal life and has even made my supervisor hint that I'm becoming unreliable.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever worry that your perceived flaws in appearance might be a sign of an underlying medical condition, or is your concern solely about the cosmetic and social implications of how you look?\n\nPatient: My concern is entirely about the cosmetic aspect and how others perceive me, rather than any kind of medical illness. My primary care doctor actually ran physical exams and found everything was completely normal. I've mostly just been trying to manage everything on my own by using makeup and changing my outfits to cover things up.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your primary concern is the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive by others, or if you genuinely believe that there's something fundamentally wrong with your body that needs to be fixed, even though your doctor has found nothing medically wrong?\n\nPatient: Since my primary care doctor found me physically healthy, I know it's not a medical disease. My distress is purely about how I look—I feel completely consumed by how old, sagging, and worn-out my face and neck appear. I'm constantly worried that others at work and in public are noticing these flaws and judging me, even when they tell me they don't see anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that others actually notice and care about the signs of aging on your face and neck as much as you do, or do you believe they are just being polite when they tell you that you look fine?\n\nPatient: I honestly believe they are just being polite to spare my feelings. I have this deep-seated feeling that everyone at work must be noticing how old and worn-out I look, even if they claim otherwise just to make me feel better.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance are more about fearing you have a serious illness or condition that's making you look old, or is it purely about the cosmetic and social impact of how you look to others?\n\nPatient: It is purely about the cosmetic and social impact, not because I'm worried about having a medical illness. I am deeply self-conscious about looking old, worn-out, and sagging, and my main dread is that others will notice these flaws and judge me. That fear is exactly why I've been avoiding presentations at work, video calls, and social gatherings.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any periods in your life where your concerns about your appearance significantly decreased or disappeared for a while, only to return later?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really had ups and downs or periods where this went away and came back. It has just been a gradual, steady worsening over the last few years as I've gotten older and taken on a more public role at work. Before this started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and didn't worry about my appearance at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any other aspects of your appearance, besides the signs of aging on your face and neck, that you are excessively concerned about or spend a significant amount of time thinking about?\n\nPatient: Yes, I also worry about my arms looking older and flabby. That's a big reason why I spend so much time changing outfits every morning, trying to find clothes that cover both my neck and my arms before I go out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your excessive concerns about your appearance, particularly the signs of aging, interfere with your daily life, relationships, and overall well-being, and do you feel that these concerns are disproportionate to any actual flaws in your appearance?\n\nPatient: These concerns have completely disrupted my life; I show up late to work, turn down presentations, avoid video calls, cancel book club, and constantly strain my marriage by begging my husband for reassurance. I'm constantly worried that others at work and in public are noticing these flaws and judging me, even when they tell me they don't see anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that others actually notice and care about the signs of aging on your face and neck as much as you do, or do you believe they are just being polite when they tell you that you look fine?\n\nPatient: I honestly believe they are just being polite to spare my feelings. I have this deep-seated feeling that everyone at work must be noticing how old and worn-out I look, even if they claim otherwise just to make me feel better.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance are more about fearing you have a serious illness or condition that's making you look old, or is it purely about the cosmetic and social impact of how you look to others?\n\nPatient: It is purely about the cosmetic and social impact, not because I'm worried about having a medical illness. I am deeply self-conscious about looking old, worn-out, and sagging, and my main dread is that others will notice these flaws and judge me. That fear is exactly why I've been avoiding presentations at work, video calls, and social gatherings.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any periods in your life where your concerns about your appearance significantly decreased or disappeared for a while, only to return later?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really had ups and downs or periods where this went away and came back. It has just been a gradual, steady worsening over the last few years as I've gotten older and taken on a more public role at work. Before this started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and didn't worry about my appearance at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any other aspects of your appearance, besides the signs of aging on your face and neck, that you are excessively concerned about or spend a significant amount of time thinking about?\n\nPatient: Yes, I also worry about my arms looking older and flabby. That's a big reason why I spend so much time changing outfits every morning, trying to find clothes that cover both my neck and my arms before I go out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your excessive concerns about your appearance, particularly the signs of aging, interfere with your daily life, relationships, and overall well-being, and do you feel that these concerns are disproportionate to any actual flaws in your appearance?\n\nPatient: These concerns have completely disrupted my life; I show up late to work, turn down presentations, avoid video calls, cancel book club, and constantly strain my marriage by begging my husband for reassurance. Even though my husband and coworkers insist they don't see what I see, the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck feel absolutely catastrophic and obvious to me. It is incredibly hard to accept their reassurance because the flaws feel so real and impossible to ignore.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you could fix or hide the perceived flaws in your appearance, you would still worry about other aspects of yourself or your life, or would your overall anxiety and distress significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest. Right now, I am so consumed by how my face and neck look that it is hard to even imagine what my life would be like without these worries. Still, I really feel like fixing these flaws would make a huge difference and take away most of my distress.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your appearance concerns are definitely related to your fear of being judged as old and unattractive, rather than a belief that there's something medically wrong with your body that needs to be fixed or corrected?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is definitely about the fear of looking old and being judged as unattractive, not a medical illness. My primary care doctor already did physical exams and found everything to be normal, so I know I'm not physically sick. Still, I just can't stop worrying about these sagging lines and my drooping neck making me look so worn-out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe in detail a typical day, including how much time you spend on your appearance concerns and how it affects your daily routines and interactions with others?"

My distress is completely focused on the signs of aging, like the sagging skin on my neck and face. I just feel completely overwhelmed by how collapsed and worn-out my face looks, and I simply dread having other people see me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could somehow completely fix or hide the signs of aging on your face and neck, your anxiety and distress would significantly decrease or even disappear?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely, because my anxiety, avoiding work, and those long morning routines are entirely driven by how I look. I truly believe that if I could just fix or hide the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck, all of this distress would disappear and my life would go right back to normal.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a specific situation where you felt your appearance was acceptable or you didn't worry about it, and how that differed from your current experiences?\n\nPatient: I can't really think of a specific situation recently where I felt my appearance was acceptable. But in the past, before these aging concerns started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and simply didn't think or worry about my looks at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about your appearance or engaging in behaviors to try to improve it, and how has this impacted your daily life and relationships?\n\nPatient: Every morning I lose nearly an hour stuck in front of the mirror applying makeup, checking my phone camera, and constantly asking my husband for reassurance. This has caused me to show up late to work, turn down important presentations, and cancel social plans like my book club. It is really straining my personal life and has even made my supervisor hint that I'm becoming unreliable.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever worry that your perceived flaws in appearance might be a sign of an underlying medical condition, or is your concern solely about the cosmetic and social implications of how you look?\n\nPatient: My concern is entirely about the cosmetic aspect and how others perceive me, rather than any kind of medical illness. My primary care doctor actually ran physical exams and found everything was completely normal. All of my distress is really just about looking so \"old and worn-out\" and the constant fear of others noticing these signs of aging on my face and neck.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have ever considered or sought cosmetic procedures, such as plastic surgery, to address your concerns about your appearance?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really sought out or seriously considered plastic surgery or cosmetic procedures. I've mostly just been trying to manage everything on my own by using makeup and changing my outfits to cover things up.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your primary concern is the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive by others, or if you genuinely believe that there's something fundamentally wrong with your body that needs to be fixed, even though your doctor has found nothing medically wrong?\n\nPatient: Since my primary care doctor found me physically healthy, I know it's not a medical disease. My distress is purely about how I look—I feel completely consumed by how old, sagging, and worn-out my face and neck appear. I'm constantly worried that others at work and in public are noticing these flaws and judging me, even when they tell me they don't see anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that others actually notice and care about the signs of aging on your face and neck as much as you do, or do you believe they are just being polite when they tell you that you look fine?\n\nPatient: I honestly believe they are just being polite to spare my feelings. I have this deep-seated feeling that everyone at work must be noticing how old and worn-out I look, even if they claim otherwise just to make me feel better.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance are more about fearing you have a serious illness or condition that's making you look old, or is it purely about the cosmetic and social impact of how you look to others?\n\nPatient: It is purely about the cosmetic and social impact, not because I'm worried about having a medical illness. I am deeply self-conscious about looking old, worn-out, and sagging, and my main dread is that others will notice these flaws and judge me. That fear is exactly why I've been avoiding presentations at work, video calls, and social gatherings.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any periods in your life where your concerns about your appearance significantly decreased or disappeared for a while, only to return later?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really had ups and downs or periods where this went away and came back. It has just been a gradual, steady worsening over the last few years as I've gotten older and taken on a more public role at work. Before this started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and didn't worry about my appearance at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any other aspects of your appearance, besides the signs of aging on your face and neck, that you are excessively concerned about or spend a significant amount of time thinking about?\n\nPatient: Yes, I also worry about my arms looking older and flabby. That's a big reason why I spend so much time changing outfits every morning, trying to find clothes that cover both my neck and my arms before I go out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your excessive concerns about your appearance, particularly the signs of aging, interfere with your daily life, relationships, and overall well-being, and do you feel that these concerns are disproportionate to any actual flaws in your appearance?\n\nPatient: These concerns have completely disrupted my life; I show up late to work, turn down presentations, avoid video calls, cancel book club, and constantly strain my marriage by begging my husband for reassurance. Even though my husband and coworkers insist they don't see what I see, the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck feel absolutely catastrophic and obvious to me. Still, I really feel like fixing these flaws would make a huge difference and take away most of my distress.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your appearance concerns are definitely related to your fear of being judged as old and unattractive, rather than a belief that there's something medically wrong with your body that needs to be fixed or corrected?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is definitely about the fear of looking old and being judged as unattractive, not a medical illness. My primary care doctor already did physical exams and found everything to be normal, so I know I'm not physically sick. Still, I just can't stop worrying about these sagging lines and my drooping neck making me look so worn-out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe in detail a typical day, including how much time you spend on your appearance concerns and how it affects your daily routines and interactions with others?\n\nPatient: A typical day starts with me losing nearly an hour under the bathroom light putting on and wiping off makeup, checking my face with my phone camera, changing outfits to hide my neck and arms, and begging my husband for reassurance. My primary care doctor actually ran physical exams and found everything was completely normal. All of my distress is really just about looking so \"old and worn-out\" and the constant fear of others noticing these signs of aging on my face and neck.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have ever considered or sought cosmetic procedures, such as plastic surgery, to address your concerns about your appearance?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really sought out or seriously considered plastic surgery or cosmetic procedures. I've mostly just been trying to manage everything on my own by using makeup and changing my outfits to cover things up.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your primary concern is the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive by others, or if you genuinely believe that there's something fundamentally wrong with your body that needs to be fixed, even though your doctor has found nothing medically wrong?\n\nPatient: Since my primary care doctor found me physically healthy, I know it's not a medical disease. My distress is purely about how I look—I feel completely consumed by how old, sagging, and worn-out my face and neck appear. I'm constantly worried that others at work and in public are noticing these flaws and judging me, even when they tell me they don't see anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that others actually notice and care about the signs of aging on your face and neck as much as you do, or do you believe they are just being polite when they tell you that you look fine?\n\nPatient: I honestly believe they are just being polite to spare my feelings. I have this deep-seated feeling that everyone at work must be noticing how old and worn-out I look, even if they claim otherwise just to make me feel better.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance are more about fearing you have a serious illness or condition that's making you look old, or is it purely about the cosmetic and social impact of how you look to others?\n\nPatient: It is purely about the cosmetic and social impact, not because I'm worried about having a medical illness. I am deeply self-conscious about looking old, worn-out, and sagging, and my main dread is that others will notice these flaws and judge me. That fear is exactly why I've been avoiding presentations at work, video calls, and social gatherings.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any periods in your life where your concerns about your appearance significantly decreased or disappeared for a while, only to return later?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really had ups and downs or periods where this went away and came back. It has just been a gradual, steady worsening over the last few years as I've gotten older and taken on a more public role at work. Before this started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and didn't worry about my appearance at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any other aspects of your appearance, besides the signs of aging on your face and neck, that you are excessively concerned about or spend a significant amount of time thinking about?\n\nPatient: Yes, I also worry about my arms looking older and flabby. That's a big reason why I spend so much time changing outfits every morning, trying to find clothes that cover both my neck and my arms before I go out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your excessive concerns about your appearance, particularly the signs of aging, interfere with your daily life, relationships, and overall well-being, and do you feel that these concerns are disproportionate to any actual flaws in your appearance?\n\nPatient: These concerns have completely disrupted my life; I show up late to work, turn down presentations, avoid video calls, cancel book club, and constantly strain my marriage by begging my husband for reassurance. Even though my husband and coworkers insist they don't see what I see, the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck feel absolutely catastrophic and obvious to me. It is incredibly hard to accept their reassurance because the flaws feel so real and impossible to ignore.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you could fix or hide the perceived flaws in your appearance, you would still worry about other aspects of yourself or your life, or would your overall anxiety and distress significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest. Right now, I am so consumed by how my face and neck look that it is hard to even imagine what my life would be like without these worries. Still, I really feel like fixing these flaws would make a huge difference and take away most of my distress.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your appearance concerns are definitely related to your fear of being judged as old and unattractive, rather than a belief that there's something medically wrong with your body that needs to be fixed or corrected?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is definitely about the fear of looking old and being judged as unattractive, not a medical illness. My primary care doctor already did physical exams and found everything to be normal, so I know I'm not physically sick. Still, I just can't stop worrying about these sagging lines and my drooping neck making me look so worn-out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe in detail a typical day, including how much time you spend on your appearance concerns and how it affects your daily routines and interactions with others?\n\nPatient: A typical day starts with me losing nearly an hour under the bathroom light putting on and wiping off makeup, checking my face with my phone camera, changing outfits to hide my neck and arms, and begging my husband for reassurance. Because of this, I often show up late to work—leading to my supervisor hinting about my reliability—and I end up turning down presentations and avoiding video calls. I've even canceled social plans like my book club and community workshops at the last minute because I feel like I just can't let anyone see me.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your distress is more about the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive, or if it's about a perceived flaw in your appearance that you believe needs to be fixed or hidden?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it feels like both. I am completely fixated on very specific flaws, like the sagging lines around my mouth and my neck drooping. I feel a desperate need to hide them with makeup and high collars because I am terrified that others will notice these flaws and think I look old, tired, and worn-out."

I've mostly just been trying to manage everything on my own by using makeup and changing my outfits to cover things up.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your primary concern is the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive by others, or if you genuinely believe that there's something fundamentally wrong with your body that needs to be fixed, even though your doctor has found nothing medically wrong?\n\nPatient: Since my primary care doctor found me physically healthy, I know it's not a medical disease. My distress is purely about how I look—I feel completely consumed by how old, sagging, and worn-out my face and neck appear. I'm constantly worried that others at work and in public are noticing these flaws and judging me, even when they tell me they don't see anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that others actually notice and care about the signs of aging on your face and neck as much as you do, or do you believe they are just being polite when they tell you that you look fine?\n\nPatient: I honestly believe they are just being polite to spare my feelings. I have this deep-seated feeling that everyone at work must be noticing how old and worn-out I look, even if they claim otherwise just to make me feel better.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance are more about fearing you have a serious illness or condition that's making you look old, or is it purely about the cosmetic and social impact of how you look to others?\n\nPatient: It is purely about the cosmetic and social impact, not because I'm worried about having a medical illness. I am deeply self-conscious about looking old, worn-out, and sagging, and my main dread is that others will notice these flaws and judge me. That fear is exactly why I've been avoiding presentations at work, video calls, and social gatherings.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any periods in your life where your concerns about your appearance significantly decreased or disappeared for a while, only to return later?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really had ups and downs or periods where this went away and came back. It has just been a gradual, steady worsening over the last few years as I've gotten older and taken on a more public role at work. Before this started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and didn't worry about my appearance at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any other aspects of your appearance, besides the signs of aging on your face and neck, that you are excessively concerned about or spend a significant amount of time thinking about?\n\nPatient: Yes, I also worry about my arms looking older and flabby. That's a big reason why I spend so much time changing outfits every morning, trying to find clothes that cover both my neck and my arms before I go out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your excessive concerns about your appearance, particularly the signs of aging, interfere with your daily life, relationships, and overall well-being, and do you feel that these concerns are disproportionate to any actual flaws in your appearance?\n\nPatient: These concerns have completely disrupted my life; I show up late to work, turn down presentations, avoid video calls, cancel book club, and constantly strain my marriage by begging my husband for reassurance. Even though my husband and coworkers insist they don't see what I see, the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck feel absolutely catastrophic and obvious to me. It is incredibly hard to accept their reassurance because the flaws feel so real and impossible to ignore.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you could fix or hide the perceived flaws in your appearance, you would still worry about other aspects of yourself or your life, or would your overall anxiety and distress significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest. Right now, I am so consumed by how my face and neck look that it is hard to even imagine what my life would be like without these worries. Still, I really feel like fixing these flaws would make a huge difference and take away most of my distress.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your appearance concerns are definitely related to your fear of being judged as old and unattractive, rather than a belief that there's something medically wrong with your body that needs to be fixed or corrected?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is definitely about the fear of looking old and being judged as unattractive, not a medical illness. My primary care doctor already did physical exams and found everything to be normal, so I know I'm not physically sick. Still, I just can't stop worrying about these sagging lines and my drooping neck making me look so worn-out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe in detail a typical day, including how much time you spend on your appearance concerns and how it affects your daily routines and interactions with others?\n\nPatient: A typical day starts with me losing nearly an hour under the bathroom light putting on and wiping off makeup, checking my face with my phone camera, changing outfits to hide my neck and arms, and begging my husband for reassurance. Because of this, I often show up late to work—leading to my supervisor hinting about my reliability—and I end up turning down presentations and avoiding video calls. I've even canceled social plans like my book club and community workshops at the last minute because I feel like I just can't let anyone see me.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your distress is more about the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive, or if it's about a perceived flaw in your appearance that you believe needs to be fixed or hidden?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it feels like both. I am completely fixated on very specific flaws, like the sagging lines around my mouth and my neck drooping. I feel a desperate need to hide them with makeup and high collars because I am terrified that others will notice these flaws and think I look old, tired, and worn-out.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your preoccupation with your appearance is focused solely on the signs of aging, such as wrinkles and sagging skin, or if you also worry about other aspects of your appearance, like your weight, body shape, or specific body parts?\n\nPatient: Yes, my focus is primarily on the signs of aging on my face and neck, specifically the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck. I also worry about my arms, which leads me to constantly change outfits to try and hide both my neck and arms. I don't really worry about my weight or overall body shape, just those specific areas.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your excessive concerns about your appearance are causing you significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, and are they truly ego-dystonic, meaning you recognize they are excessive or unreasonable?"

Before this started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and didn't worry about my appearance at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any other aspects of your appearance, besides the signs of aging on your face and neck, that you are excessively concerned about or spend a significant amount of time thinking about?\n\nPatient: Yes, I also worry about my arms looking older and flabby. That's a big reason why I spend so much time changing outfits every morning, trying to find clothes that cover both my neck and my arms before I go out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your excessive concerns about your appearance, particularly the signs of aging, interfere with your daily life, relationships, and overall well-being, and do you feel that these concerns are disproportionate to any actual flaws in your appearance?\n\nPatient: These concerns have completely disrupted my life; I show up late to work, turn down presentations, avoid video calls, cancel book club, and constantly strain my marriage by begging my husband for reassurance. Even though my husband and coworkers insist they don't see what I see, the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck feel absolutely catastrophic and obvious to me. It is incredibly hard to accept their reassurance because the flaws feel so real and impossible to ignore.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you could fix or hide the perceived flaws in your appearance, you would still worry about other aspects of yourself or your life, or would your overall anxiety and distress significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest. Right now, I am so consumed by how my face and neck look that it is hard to even imagine what my life would be like without these worries. Still, I really feel like fixing these flaws would make a huge difference and take away most of my distress.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your appearance concerns are definitely related to your fear of being judged as old and unattractive, rather than a belief that there's something medically wrong with your body that needs to be fixed or corrected?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is definitely about the fear of looking old and being judged as unattractive, not a medical illness. My primary care doctor already did physical exams and found everything to be normal, so I know I'm not physically sick. Still, I just can't stop worrying about these sagging lines and my drooping neck making me look so worn-out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe in detail a typical day, including how much time you spend on your appearance concerns and how it affects your daily routines and interactions with others?\n\nPatient: A typical day starts with me losing nearly an hour under the bathroom light putting on and wiping off makeup, checking my face with my phone camera, changing outfits to hide my neck and arms, and begging my husband for reassurance. Because of this, I often show up late to work—leading to my supervisor hinting about my reliability—and I end up turning down presentations and avoiding video calls. I've even canceled social plans like my book club and community workshops at the last minute because I feel like I just can't let anyone see me.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your distress is more about the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive, or if it's about a perceived flaw in your appearance that you believe needs to be fixed or hidden?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it feels like both. I am completely fixated on very specific flaws, like the sagging lines around my mouth and my neck drooping. I feel a desperate need to hide them with makeup and high collars because I am terrified that others will notice these flaws and think I look old, tired, and worn-out.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your preoccupation with your appearance is focused solely on the signs of aging, such as wrinkles and sagging skin, or if you also worry about other aspects of your appearance, like your weight, body shape, or specific body parts?\n\nPatient: Yes, my focus is primarily on the signs of aging on my face and neck, specifically the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck. I also worry about my arms, which leads me to constantly change outfits to try and hide both my neck and arms. I don't really worry about my weight or overall body shape, just those specific areas.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your excessive concerns about your appearance are causing you significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, and are they truly ego-dystonic, meaning you recognize they are excessive or unreasonable?\n\nPatient: Yes, they have completely disrupted my life; I've been turning down presentations, canceling social plans at the last minute, and running late to work to the point where my supervisor has questioned my reliability. Deep down, I do realize my reaction is getting out of hand and is probably excessive, especially since others tell me they don't see what I see. However, I still can't stop feeling this way, and it causes me immense distress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you would feel and what you would do if you were in a situation where you couldn't check your appearance or hide your perceived flaws for an entire day?\n\nPatient: Just thinking about that scenario makes me feel incredibly anxious because I would feel completely exposed, convinced that everyone was staring right at my sagging face and drooping neck. I would likely panic and try to avoid going out altogether, or if I absolutely had to, I'd be totally unable to focus on anything else and would desperately look for any way to hide or escape.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there was ever a time when you believed your appearance concerns were related to an underlying medical condition, or has it always been about the cosmetic and social impact of how you look?"

I've mostly just been trying to manage everything on my own by using makeup and changing my outfits to cover things up.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your primary concern is the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive by others, or if you genuinely believe that there's something fundamentally wrong with your body that needs to be fixed, even though your doctor has found nothing medically wrong?\n\nPatient: Since my primary care doctor found me physically healthy, I know it's not a medical disease. My distress is purely about how I look—I feel completely consumed by how old, sagging, and worn-out my face and neck appear. I'm constantly worried that others at work and in public are noticing these flaws and judging me, even when they tell me they don't see anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that others actually notice and care about the signs of aging on your face and neck as much as you do, or do you believe they are just being polite when they tell you that you look fine?\n\nPatient: I honestly believe they are just being polite to spare my feelings. I have this deep-seated feeling that everyone at work must be noticing how old and worn-out I look, even if they claim otherwise just to make me feel better.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance are more about fearing you have a serious illness or condition that's making you look old, or is it purely about the cosmetic and social impact of how you look to others?\n\nPatient: It is purely about the cosmetic and social impact, not because I'm worried about having a medical illness. I am deeply self-conscious about looking old, worn-out, and sagging, and my main dread is that others will notice these flaws and judge me. That fear is exactly why I've been avoiding presentations at work, video calls, and social gatherings.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any periods in your life where your concerns about your appearance significantly decreased or disappeared for a while, only to return later?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really had ups and downs or periods where this went away and came back. It has just been a gradual, steady worsening over the last few years as I've gotten older and taken on a more public role at work. Before this started, I had a very practical, low-fuss routine and didn't worry about my appearance at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any other aspects of your appearance, besides the signs of aging on your face and neck, that you are excessively concerned about or spend a significant amount of time thinking about?\n\nPatient: Yes, I also worry about my arms looking older and flabby. That's a big reason why I spend so much time changing outfits every morning, trying to find clothes that cover both my neck and my arms before I go out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your excessive concerns about your appearance, particularly the signs of aging, interfere with your daily life, relationships, and overall well-being, and do you feel that these concerns are disproportionate to any actual flaws in your appearance?\n\nPatient: These concerns have completely disrupted my life; I show up late to work, turn down presentations, avoid video calls, cancel book club, and constantly strain my marriage by begging my husband for reassurance. Even though my husband and coworkers insist they don't see what I see, the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck feel absolutely catastrophic and obvious to me. It is incredibly hard to accept their reassurance because the flaws feel so real and impossible to ignore.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you could fix or hide the perceived flaws in your appearance, you would still worry about other aspects of yourself or your life, or would your overall anxiety and distress significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest. Right now, I am so consumed by how my face and neck look that it is hard to even imagine what my life would be like without these worries. Still, I really feel like fixing these flaws would make a huge difference and take away most of my distress.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your appearance concerns are definitely related to your fear of being judged as old and unattractive, rather than a belief that there's something medically wrong with your body that needs to be fixed or corrected?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is definitely about the fear of looking old and being judged as unattractive, not a medical illness. My primary care doctor already did physical exams and found everything to be normal, so I know I'm not physically sick. Still, I just can't stop worrying about these sagging lines and my drooping neck making me look so worn-out.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe in detail a typical day, including how much time you spend on your appearance concerns and how it affects your daily routines and interactions with others?\n\nPatient: A typical day starts with me losing nearly an hour under the bathroom light putting on and wiping off makeup, checking my face with my phone camera, changing outfits to hide my neck and arms, and begging my husband for reassurance. Because of this, I often show up late to work—leading to my supervisor hinting about my reliability—and I end up turning down presentations and avoiding video calls. I've even canceled social plans like my book club and community workshops at the last minute because I feel like I just can't let anyone see me.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your distress is more about the fear of being perceived as old and unattractive, or if it's about a perceived flaw in your appearance that you believe needs to be fixed or hidden?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it feels like both. I am completely fixated on very specific flaws, like the sagging lines around my mouth and my neck drooping. I feel a desperate need to hide them with makeup and high collars because I am terrified that others will notice these flaws and think I look old, tired, and worn-out.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your preoccupation with your appearance is focused solely on the signs of aging, such as wrinkles and sagging skin, or if you also worry about other aspects of your appearance, like your weight, body shape, or specific body parts?\n\nPatient: Yes, my focus is primarily on the signs of aging on my face and neck, specifically the sagging lines around my mouth and my drooping neck. I also worry about my arms, which leads me to constantly change outfits to try and hide both my neck and arms. I don't really worry about my weight or overall body shape, just those specific areas.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your excessive concerns about your appearance are causing you significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, and are they truly ego-dystonic, meaning you recognize they are excessive or unreasonable?\n\nPatient: Yes, they have completely disrupted my life; I've been turning down presentations, canceling social plans at the last minute, and running late to work to the point where my supervisor has questioned my reliability. Deep down, I do realize my reaction is getting out of hand and is probably excessive, especially since others tell me they don't see what I see. However, I still can't stop feeling this way, and it causes me immense distress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you would feel and what you would do if you were in a situation where you couldn't check your appearance or hide your perceived flaws for an entire day?\n\nPatient: Just thinking about that scenario makes me feel incredibly anxious because I would feel completely exposed, convinced that everyone was staring right at my sagging face and drooping neck. I would likely panic and try to avoid going out altogether, or if I absolutely had to, I'd be totally unable to focus on anything else and would desperately look for any way to hide or escape.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there was ever a time when you believed your appearance concerns were related to an underlying medical condition, or has it always been about the cosmetic and social impact of how you look?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really thought of it as an underlying medical condition. For me, it has always felt like it's just about the physical signs of aging and how they affect my appearance and social interactions, rather than a medical illness.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have any other recurring, intrusive thoughts or compulsions to perform specific rituals or behaviors outside of your appearance concerns?\n\nPatient: No, I don't experience any other recurring, intrusive thoughts or ritualistic behaviors outside of my concerns about aging. All of my worries and daily routines are strictly focused on how my face, neck, and arms look.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your excessive concerns about your appearance are driven by a desire to improve your overall appearance or to specifically fix perceived flaws that you believe are noticeable to others?"
